pg086_n0035: A salad is a cold dish which is made by using a mixture of raw or cooked vegetables and fruits sometimes accompanied by meat or fish.
pg086_n0036: It can be dressed with oil, vinegar, or other dressings.
pg086_n0037: Salads make the meal attractive, stimulating and appetising.
pg086_n0038: Since salads are made using vegetables and fruits, they provide essential nutrients to the body.
pg086_n0039: The amount of nutrients in salads depends on the ingredients and the preparation method.
pg086_n0040: It also depends on whether they are eaten raw or cooked.
pg086_n0041: Cooking may reduce levels of some nutrients such as vitamin B and C.
pg086_n0042: Salad can be served as a starter to a meal, an accompaniment to a main meal or as a filling to food.
pg086_n0043: Salad ingredients include green vegetables such as lettuce, cabbage and spinach; other vegetables such as carrots, onions, celery, cauliflower and peas.
pg086_n0044: Examples of salad dishes are fruit and vegetable salad, arranged vegetable salads and mixed cooked vegetable salads.
pg087_n0006: Besides their nutritional value, salads add colour to a prepared meal.
pg087_n0007: A meal with a salad is appetising, making an individual eat enough food and satisfy hunger.
pg087_n0008: The following are the benefits of salads in the body.
pg087_n0010: Salads provide enough vitamins and minerals.
pg087_n0011: The consumption of fruits and vegetables provides enough vitamins and minerals to maintain a healthy body and mind.
pg087_n0012: Salads are also full of flavour and have a satisfying crunch.
pg087_n0013: They are rich in antioxidants such as carotenoids, and vitamins C and E.
pg087_n0014: Hence, salads can protect the body against various types of cancer.
pg087_n0017: Fibre prevents constipation by softening human excrement.
pg087_n0018: Fibre also lowers body cholesterol and regulates blood sugar, hence preventing the risk of heart disease and diabetes.
pg087_n0019: Salads satisfy hunger as they make someone feel full for a long time.
pg087_n0020: Adding a healthy salad to every meal can facilitate weight management.
pg087_n0021: For example, a salad made with a large serving of spinach and kale creates a strong foundation for weight loss.
pg087_n0025: For example, a salad with olive oil and avocados contain healthy fats which lower cholesterol level, hence reducing the risk of heart disease.
pg087_n0028: Salads contain sufficient amounts of water for the body to perform various functions.
pg087_n0029: Watermelon and strawberries, for instance, contain 92 per cent of water; likewise, cucumbers and certain lettuces contain 96 per cent of water.
pg087_n0030: Salads made with a combination of vegetables and fruits supplies water to the body.
pg087_n0031: Grapefruits, peaches, oranges, pineapples, spinach, broccoli, and tomatoes are other fruits and vegetables with high water content.

pg093_n0026: Food decoration involves adding edible material to a sweet dish to enrich or beautify it.
pg093_n0027: Food decoration enhances meal presentation, whereas undecorated foods make meals look quite unattractive.
pg093_n0028: Food decoration process involves topping with icing and jam or designing ornamental decorations such as edible silver balls.
pg093_n0029: Most decorations require no or little preparation before use.
pg093_n0030: For example, jam does not require any preparation to decorate a dish such as steamed jam pudding.
pg093_n0031: Items that can decorate dishes include cherries, sweets, nuts, fruits, sugar, icings, whipping creams, strawberries, and jam.
pg094_n0003: Garnishing involves adding decorative edible ingredients to a savoury dish before serving it.
pg094_n0004: Examples of garnishes include parsley leaves, shredded lettuce, sliced cucumber and grated carrots.
pg094_n0005: They can be used in their raw states or cooked.
pg094_n0006: Garnishes add flavour and nutrients to the dish.
pg094_n0007: They improve colour and add an attractive appearance to dishes.
pg094_n0008: One should consider the following points when garnishing or decorating dishes:
pg094_n0012: The colour effect of garnishes or decorations should not dominate the colour of dishes.
pg094_n0015: Some garnishes such as carrot and sweet pepper may undergo a blanching process to kill microbes before use.
pg094_n0018: Arrange garnishes and decorations neatly to get the overall effect.
pg094_n0021: Vary colours and types of garnishes or decorations to avoid monotonous meal appearances.
pg094_n0024: The flavour of a garnish or decoration should not interfere with that of the dish.

pg100_n0008: Beverages and appetizers nourish the body by providing the necessary nutrients for health.
pg100_n0009: Beverages and appetizers can be either liquid or solid foods.
pg100_n0010: Some fruits and vegetables are used to make beverages and appetizers.
pg100_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn about beverages and appetizers, their types and how to prepare them.
pg100_n0012: You will also learn about the negative effects of beverages.
pg100_n0013: The competencies developed will enable you to prepare various beverages and appetizers for individual and family use or business purposes.
pg100_n0017: The roles and kinds of beverages and appetizers found in our society
pg100_n0021: Beverages are hot or cold drinks which are specifically prepared for human consumption.
pg100_n0022: They are served as drinks with or without meals.
pg100_n0023: Examples of beverages are tea, coffee, milk, coconut milk, alcoholic drinks and soft drinks such as fruits and carbonated drinks.
pg100_n0024: Some beverages provide nutrients to our bodies and maintain body fluid levels.
pg100_n0025: Selecting beverages is based on age, lifestyle, the weather, health condition, and occasion.
pg100_n0026: The following points show the importance of taking beverages:
pg100_n0031: Beverages provide essential fluids for hydrating body organs such as the eyes, nose, mouth and lungs as well as tissues for them to function properly.
pg100_n0032: However, some beverages such as alcohol and concentrated coffee have diuretic effects; they remove fluids from the body and cause dehydration.
pg100_n0035: They replace the water lost from the body through sweating, excretion and breathing, hence, they help maintaining the level of body fluids.
pg100_n0038: Beverages help us to quench our thirst.
pg101_n0005: They nourish the body by providing nutrients.
pg101_n0008: They regulate body metabolic processes such as digestion.
pg101_n0012: They aid in food movement along the gut, thus preventing constipation.
pg101_n0015: They are also included as an important accompaniment in meals for invalids, small children, and the elderly as such meals are easily digested.
pg101_n0018: They provide social function roles as they are served at most meetings and are a part of expressing hospitality.
pg101_n0024: Beverages stimulate one’s appetite for food.
pg101_n0025: For example, soup can be used as an appetizer for stimulating appetite.
pg101_n0028: Many beverages contain carbohydrates or caffeine which can provide a quick energy boost.
pg101_n0031: Cold beverages like sodas and fruit juices can be refreshing, especially during hot weather.
pg101_n0035: Beverages are classified into three main groups, namely refreshing or thirsty-quenching drinks, stimulating drinks and nourishing drinks.
pg101_n0039: Refreshing drinks are beverages that are used when a person is feeling thirsty or seeking relief from heat or dehydration.
pg101_n0040: These drinks are typically cold or chilled and are known for their ability to quench thirst by providing a pleasant sensation of refreshment.
pg101_n0041: Some popular examples of refreshing and thirst-quenching drinks include punch and all types of juice from fruits such as passion, pineapples, and mangoes or vegetables such as carrots.
pg101_n0042: Some beverages not only refresh but also provide the body with nutrients.
pg101_n0043: Hence, their consumption is strongly encouraged.
pg101_n0044: Most fruit and vegetable juices contain high levels of vitamins A, E and C and minerals such as potassium and sodium.
pg101_n0045: Refreshing drinks also hydrate the body; thus, they alleviate dehydration-related symptoms such as thirst, mouth dryness and mental fatigue.
pg101_n0046: The following are points to consider when preparing fruit juice:
pg101_n0050: Prepare fruit juice just before use to prevent it from spoilage or loss of vitamins such as vitamin C.
pg102_n0006: Sugar or syrup may or may not be added to fruit juice, depending on personal preferences.
pg102_n0007: However, juice with added sugar adds to the levels of calories, resulting in weight gain.
pg102_n0008: The choice of using either syrup or sugar in making juice is entirely up to personal preference and convenience.
pg102_n0009: Some people prefer to use syrup since it mixes easily and quickly.
pg102_n0010: Others may prefer granulated sugar when they want to have more control over the sweetness level.
pg102_n0011: While sugar can certainly sweeten the juice effectively, it may require more effort to ensure that the sugar is fully dissolved and evenly distributed in the juice.
pg102_n0015: When using more than one fruit type to make fruit juice, consider including the one with a sharp taste to enrich the flavour of the final drink.
pg102_n0019: If the drink is to be served cold, chill it in a refrigerator or add ice-cubes just before serving.
pg102_n0023: Do not use metal containers when making or storing acidic juice as ascorbic acids from fruits react with metal from the container resulting in a metallic taste.
pg102_n0027: Garnish the juice with a slice of the fruit used in making it or its plant’s part or any other flavourful leaves, such as mint leaves, before serving.

pg111_n0005: Common examples of these stimulating drinks include coffee, tea and cocoa.

pg114_n0007: Nourishing drinks can be made using a variety of natural ingredients, including fruits, vegetables, herbs, nuts, seeds, and dairy or plant-based milk alternatives.
pg114_n0008: Some common examples of nourishing drinks include fruit juice, milk, soup, yoghurt, enriched porridge and smoothies.
pg114_n0009: Nourishing drinks are important for a person who has lost appetite due to an illness.

pg116_n0029: Beverages play significant roles in our bodies; however, unhealthy beverages may have some negative effects.
pg116_n0030: These beverages include artificially sweetened juice, carbonated drinks and alcoholic drinks.
pg116_n0031: These drinks have adverse impacts on body health when consumed in excess.
pg116_n0032: For example, they may cause overweight and obesity and increase the risk of non-communicable diseases, such as cardiovascular diseases and type 2 diabetes.
pg116_n0033: Overconsumption of caffeine and tannin in coffee and tea may also lead to stimulating and dehydrating effects on the body, particularly anxiety and insomnia.
pg116_n0034: Likewise, pregnant women should reduce or avoid consuming caffeinated drinks, because they may increase the risk of miscarriage.
pg116_n0036: Alcoholic beverages have both stimulating and depressing effects.
pg116_n0037: They are stimulants because they alert, awake and energise the body.
pg117_n0005: may slow down neural activities and brain functioning, resulting in depressing effects.
pg117_n0006: Overconsumption of alcohol may lead to social and health problems.
pg117_n0007: Social problems include alcohol addiction, increased crime and reduced working ability.
pg117_n0008: Health problems include overweight, obesity, liver cirrhosis and high blood pressure.
pg117_n0012: An appetizer is a solid or liquid food taken before a main meal to stimulate the appetite.
pg117_n0013: An appetizer is also known as a starter and is usually served in small portions.
pg117_n0014: Appetizers are often savoury and flavourful, designed to stimulate the taste buds and leave eaters excited for the rest of the meal.
pg117_n0015: Appetizers can take various forms, and their preparation can vary depending on cultural and regional culinary traditions.
pg117_n0019: There are several types of appetizers.
pg117_n0020: The commonest ones include cocktails, mocktails, Hors d’oeuvres and soups.
pg117_n0024: A cocktail is a drink prepared by using different drinks, one of them being an alcoholic drink.
pg117_n0025: Cocktails are usually served as a first-course meal.
pg117_n0026: They can be prepared by blending, shaking and stirring methods.
pg117_n0027: An example of a cocktail drink is a fruit punch.
pg117_n0031: A mocktail is a non-alcoholic beverage resembling a cocktail in appearance, presentation, and flavour.
pg117_n0032: It includes the addition of different fruits, syrup, juices, or cream.
pg117_n0033: Mocktails are designed to provide the same enjoyable and refreshing experience as cocktails, but without alcohol.
pg117_n0034: Mocktails are an excellent alternative for individuals who choose not to consume alcohol, including pregnant women, designated drivers, and those who prefer non-alcoholic options for various reasons.
pg117_n0035: They are also suitable for social gatherings where guests of all ages can participate in the celebration without alcohol.
pg117_n0036: Like cocktails, mocktails can come in various flavours and styles, using a wide range of ingredients such as fruit juices, syrups, carbonated drinks, fresh fruits, herbs and spices.
pg117_n0037: Mocktails are often garnished with fruits, herbs, and colourful straws making them visually appealing and enjoyable.
pg117_n0038: Examples of mocktails include an orange, pineapple and lemonade drink as well as a mint and ginger lemon drink.
pg118_n0005: The preparation of a mocktail is straightforward and enjoyable.
pg118_n0006: The preparation of a mocktail requires non-alcoholic drinks such as fruit juices and carbonated drinks.
pg118_n0007: A sweetener (optional), such as syrup, honey, or fruit syrups, may be added to enhance the flavour.
pg118_n0008: Flavourings such as herbs, spices, or syrups are added to create unique and refreshing flavours.
pg118_n0009: Ice cubes or refrigerators are essential for chilling mocktails.

pg124_n0022: Stock is a flavourful liquid that forms the base or foundation of many types of soups, sauces, stews, and other dishes.
pg124_n0023: It enhances good taste and texture of the final dish.
pg124_n0024: Stock is made from bones, meat, fish, or vegetables with aromatic ingredients in water.
pg124_n0025: Some vegetables are not suitable for making stock.
pg124_n0026: These are potatoes and green leafy vegetables.
pg124_n0027: Potatoes cause sour taste stock, and green leafy vegetables cause bitter taste stock.
pg124_n0028: The stock is made by the simmering method.
pg124_n0029: This is a method where food is cooked gently and slowly.
pg124_n0030: The slow simmering process extracts the flavours, nutrients, and gelatin from the ingredients, resulting in a rich and savoury liquid.
pg124_n0031: The nutritional value of stock depends on the ingredients used.
pg124_n0032: The following are points to consider when preparing stock for soups:
pg124_n0035: (a) Use clean and fresh ingredients for making stock.
pg124_n0037: (b) Cut fish or meat into small pieces to facilitate flavour extraction.
pg124_n0039: (c) Cover the ingredients with cold water and cook using a simmering method.
pg124_n0041: (d) To concentrate the flavour, remove the lid to let the water evaporate.
pg124_n0043: (e) Skim the stock to remove excess fat.
pg124_n0045: (f) Strain the stock when ready, cool quickly, and store it in a cool place.
pg124_n0048: You can refrigerate the stock for up to three days.
pg124_n0050: (h) Do not warm the stock more than once as this will create an ideal condition for bacterial growth.
pg124_n0052: (i) Cook meat stock for a longer duration than you do for vegetable stock to extract the maximum flavour, nutrients, and gelatin from the meat and bones.
pg125_n0005: Soup is a well-flavoured nutritious liquid served at the beginning of a meal.
pg125_n0006: It is made from stocks of vegetables, meat, fish, grains and pulses.
pg125_n0007: Soup is an important appetiser in the meal.
pg125_n0009: Most of the soups provide heat to the body, especially in the cold season.
pg125_n0013: Simmering is a cooking technique that involves cooking food gently and slowly in a liquid at a temperature just below boiling point.
pg125_n0014: When simmering, the liquid should be kept at a temperature where small bubbles occasionally rise to the surface and break gently.
pg125_n0015: The exact temperature for simmering is around 180°F to 200°F (82°C to 93°C).
pg125_n0016: Simmering is a common cooking method used for a variety of dishes, including soups, stews, sauces, and certain braised dishes.
pg125_n0017: It allows for gentle and even cooking, ensuring that the flavours blend while preserving the texture of the ingredients.
pg125_n0018: When cooking by the simmering method, consider the following points:
pg125_n0022: Cover the pot with a lid to retain moisture and heat, allowing the food to cook evenly and preventing excessive evaporation of the liquid.
pg125_n0025: Do not open the pot unless you are sure that the simmering is ready.
pg125_n0028: Keep the temperature at a point just below boiling.
pg125_n0029: If the food is about to boil, add an extra broth or cooking liquid to cool it.
pg125_n0032: Use a pot that is large enough to hold all the ingredients comfortably without overcrowding.
pg125_n0033: This allows the liquid to circulate the ingredients and ensures even cooking.
pg125_n0036: Stir the food occasionally while simmering to prevent sticking or burning, especially for dishes with thick sauces or starchy components.
pg125_n0039: Simmering is a slow cooking method, so be patient and allow the ingredients to cook fully.
pg125_n0040: The cooking time will vary depending on the dish and the ingredients used.
pg125_n0043: The liquid used for simmering, such as stock, broth, or sauce, is essential for infusing flavour into the food.
pg125_n0044: Season the liquid with flavourings such as herbs and spices to enhance the overall taste and aroma of the dish.
pg125_n0047: When simmering is complete, leave the dish for a few minutes before serving.
pg125_n0048: This allows the flavours to develop further and ensures that the food is at an ideal serving temperature.
pg126_n0007: Flavour infusion: Simmering allows the flavours of the ingredients to blend together, creating a harmonious and tasty dish.
pg126_n0010: Tenderizing: For tougher cuts of meat or fibrous vegetables, simmering helps to break down the connective tissues and fibres, making the food more tender and easier to chew.
pg126_n0013: Reduction: Simmering helps to reduce the liquid in a dish, concentrating the flavours and creating a thicker and more flavourful sauce or broth.
pg126_n0016: Even Cooking: The gentle and consistent heat of simmering ensures that the food cooks evenly without becoming overcooked or burnt.
pg126_n0020: While simmering is a widely used and effective cooking method for many dishes, it has some disadvantages:
pg126_n0024: Time-consuming: Simmering is a slow cooking process, and some dishes may require extended periods to be cooked thoroughly.
pg126_n0027: Potential of overcooking: If not closely monitored, there is a risk of overcooking certain ingredients during simmering.
pg126_n0028: Overcooked vegetables may lose their texture and become mushy, while meats can become dry and tough.
pg126_n0031: Evaporation of liquid: During simmering, some of the liquid in the dish can evaporate.
pg126_n0032: While this can lead to a concentration of flavours, it can also reduce the amount of sauce or broth, which might not be desirable in certain recipes.
pg126_n0035: Unsuitable for certain ingredients: Simmering may not be suitable for some delicate vegetables as they can become overcooked and lose their vibrant colours, crispness, and nutritional value.
pg126_n0036: It may affect the texture and flavour.
pg126_n0039: Slow flavour infusion: While simmering allows for flavour infusion, it may not be as rapid as other cooking methods like boiling or steaming.
pg126_n0040: Hence, certain herbs and spices may not release their flavours as quickly as desired.

pg127_n0023: Soups can be broadly classified into four classes, namely thin, thick, cold and international soups.
pg127_n0028: Thin soups are prepared without a thickening agent.
pg127_n0029: They may be served plain or garnished with solid ingredients such as vegetables, fish, pasta, and meat.
pg127_n0030: Thin soups can be strained or unstrained.
pg127_n0031: They include clear soup, broth and consommé.
pg127_n0033: Clear soup: This is a clear, transparent and flavoured soup.
pg127_n0034: It can be made from poultry, beef or vegetables.
pg127_n0035: It has no solid ingredients because it is strained after preparation.
pg127_n0036: The soup is thin like liquid.
pg127_n0037: This soup is simple to prepare.
pg127_im066: Bowl of clear golden soup with no solid ingredients visible.
pg127_sec001_ans_item-1: He can use vegetables such as carrots, onions, tomatoes, cabbage, spinach, green pepper and celery.
pg127_sec001_ans_item-2: He can use flavourings such as salt, onions, garlic, curry powder, black pepper and stock cubes.
pg127_sec001_ans_item-3: Use the boiling or simmering method: wash and cut the vegetables, boil them in water or stock, add seasoning, then simmer until tender and strain if a clear soup is needed.
pg127_sec001_ans_item-4: This method softens the vegetables, extracts flavour and nutrients into the soup, makes it easy to digest and is simple to prepare.
pg127_sec001_ans_item-5: Ingredients needed include vegetables, water or stock, salt, onions, tomatoes, garlic, cooking oil or butter, pepper and stock cubes.
pg127_sec001_ans_item-6: It is best consumed while hot, especially at lunch or dinner, or as a starter before the main meal.
pg128_n0003: Broth: This soup is similar to clear soup, except that it is not strained.
pg128_n0004: It also has solid ingredients such as small pieces of vegetables, fish, meat, rice, pasta or oats.
pg128_n0005: The preparation of broth is similar to that of clear soup.
pg128_n0006: Examples of broth soups are beef broth, vegetable broth and fish broth.
pg128_im056: Bowl of broth soup with clear brown stock, small pieces of meat, vegetables and short pasta.
pg128_n0011: Consommé: This is a light clear soup that is made with concentrated beef or chicken stock and served hot.
pg128_n0012: Egg white is added to the soup before serving.
pg128_im058: Shallow bowl of consommé soup, smooth and yellow, sprinkled with small green herb pieces.
pg128_n0019: Thick soups are thickened using flour, cornstarch, cream, vegetables, gelatines and other ingredients.
pg128_n0020: Unlike thin soups, thick soups are opaque.
pg128_n0021: They can have different textures and flavours depending on the thickening ingredients used.
pg128_n0022: Thick soups are classified as puree soup, cream soup, chowders, bisque and velouté.
pg129_n0004: Puree soups: These are made by simmering dried or fresh starchy vegetables in stock or water.
pg129_n0005: Thereafter, they are blended or crushed to form a thick consistency, called puree soup.
pg129_n0006: The ingredients in the pureed soup are typically cooked until soft and then blended until smooth, resulting in a heavy consistency texture with no visible pieces of food materials.
pg129_n0007: They may be made from rice, dried legumes such as peas, or fresh starchy vegetables such as potatoes.
pg129_n0008: Some common ingredients used to make puree soups include vegetables like tomatoes, carrots, potatoes, peas, or cauliflower.
pg129_n0009: Fruits like apples, pears, or pumpkins can also be used in sweet puree soups.
pg129_n0010: Figure 5.19 shows a puree of vegetable soup.
pg129_im062: Bowl of thick orange pureed vegetable soup garnished with chopped herbs.
pg129_n0014: Cream soups: Cream soups are a type of soup known for their rich and creamy texture.
pg129_n0015: They are achieved by incorporating dairy products such as cream, milk, or butter into the soup.
pg129_n0016: These soups are smooth and soft in consistency.
pg129_n0017: Cream soups can be made with a variety of ingredients, including vegetables, cream, seafood, poultry, or meat.
pg129_n0018: They are seasoned with herbs, spices, and other flavourings to enhance their taste.
pg129_n0019: Examples of cream soup include tomato soup, mushroom soup and chicken soup.
pg129_n0020: Figure 5.20 shows the cream of mushroom soup.
pg129_im063: Shallow bowl of cream of mushroom soup with visible mushroom pieces and a light herb garnish.
pg130_n0003: Chowders: These are thick soups made with large pieces (chunky) of food materials, typically made by combining various ingredients such as fish, seafood, poultry, or vegetables with a creamy base.
pg130_n0004: They are typically seasoned with herbs, spices, and sometimes bacon or salt pork to enhance their flavour.
pg130_n0006: Examples of chowders are seafood chowder soup and maize chowder soup.
pg130_n0007: Figure 5.21 presents maize chowder soup, also known as corn chowder.
pg130_im056: Bowl of creamy maize chowder with sweetcorn kernels, small vegetable pieces and a parsley garnish.
pg130_n0011: Bisque: It is a shellfish-based soup with a variety of flavouring ingredients added.
pg130_n0012: Traditionally, bisque is made with lobster, crab, shrimp, or crawfish, but there are also variations using vegetables, mushrooms, or other seafood.
pg130_n0013: Bisque soup is tasty but expensive.
pg130_n0014: The soup may be garnished with dice of the seafood used.
pg130_n0015: It is thickened with cooked rice and finished with cream.
pg130_n0016: Examples of bisque soups are lobster and prawn bisque.
pg130_im058: Bowl of smooth orange prawn bisque topped with a whole prawn and sprinkled with chopped herbs.
pg131_n0004: Velouté: A velouté is a thick soup.
pg131_n0005: It is made from meat, poultry, fish or vegetables.
pg131_n0006: Its flavour is determined by the stock used.
pg131_n0007: The soup is thickened with a blond, which is made by cooking equal amounts of wheat flour and butter over medium heat until light brown.
pg131_n0008: Egg yolks and cream are added to this soup just before serving.
pg131_n0009: Velouté is incredibly versatile and serves as the base for many delicious dishes, both as a sauce and as a soup.
pg131_n0010: The specific name of the soup depends on the stock used; for example, chicken velouté soup is made with chicken.
pg131_n0014: Cold soups, also known as chilled soups, are a refreshing and appetizing culinary option, especially during hot weather.
pg131_n0015: They constitute a special category because they are served chilled.
pg131_n0016: Hot soups become cold soups after undergoing chilling with minor alterations made to their consistency and flavour.
pg131_n0017: Cold soups can be thickened with starches.
pg131_n0018: These soups are more popular in warm weather.
pg131_n0019: Unlike traditional hot soups, which are served warm, cold soups are meant to be enjoyed cold or at room temperature.
pg131_n0023: International soups, also known as national soups, include various types of flavourful and unique soup recipes from various countries and cultures around the world.
pg131_n0024: They represent the region of origin.
pg131_n0025: Each soup reflects the culinary traditions, regional ingredients, and local preferences of its country of origin.
pg131_n0026: They significantly reflect a particular culture and history.
pg131_n0027: They are valued as a symbol of national identity.
pg131_n0028: Examples are scotch broth from Scotland, green turtle soup from England and French onion soup from France.

pg134_n0010: Pulses, nuts and oil seeds are foods that contain nutrients such as protein, fat, minerals and vitamins, which are necessary for our bodies.
pg134_n0011: Pulses and nuts also contain beneficial dietary fibres.
pg134_n0012: They are used to make various dishes using different cooking methods.
pg134_n0013: They are found in various shapes, sizes and colours.
pg134_n0014: In this chapter, you will learn about the concepts of pulses, nuts and oil seeds, the nutritive values of pulses and nuts, their uses and the methods of cooking them.
pg134_n0015: The competencies developed will enable you to use pulses, nuts and oil seeds in making different dishes to improve health and earn income.
pg134_n0018: Various ways in which pulses, nuts and oil seeds can be used
pg134_n0023: They are also known as legumes.
pg134_n0024: Pulses are valued for their nutritional value, affordability and availability.
pg134_n0025: They are low in fat, high in protein, and rich in dietary fibre, making them an excellent source of plant-based protein and other essential nutrients.
pg134_n0026: The commonly used pulses are beans, cowpeas, soya beans, chickpeas, green grams, lima beans, lentils, Bambara nuts and pigeon peas.
pg134_n0027: Like beans, lentils, and chickpeas, pulses have an outer protective layer called a seed coat or skin.
pg134_n0028: Over time, especially in storage conditions with fluctuating temperatures and humidity, the seed coat of pulses can become harder and less permeable, making it difficult to cook.
pg134_n0029: Figure 6.1 shows different types of pulses.
pg136_n0005: Pulses contain essential nutrients such as proteins of low biological value and B-vitamins (except for riboflavin) as well as minerals such as iron, potassium and magnesium.
pg136_n0006: Pulses contain carbohydrates but in low amounts.
pg136_n0007: They are also low in fat content, except for soya beans which are a very good source of fat.
pg136_n0008: Pulses are also rich in dietary fibre.
pg136_n0012: Pulses are used in making gravies, stews, soups and bites.
pg136_n0013: They can also be used to make salads and desserts.
pg136_n0014: They can be ground to fine powder and used in thickening and adding extra protein to the meal.
pg136_n0015: In vegetarian meals, cooked pulses are the main source of protein.
pg136_n0016: Pulses can also be served with other starchy foods such as ugali, rice and pasta.
pg136_n0020: Nuts are seeds enclosed in shells.
pg136_n0021: These are highly nutritious and healthy foods that can provide a wide range of essential nutrients and health benefits.
pg136_n0022: They are good sources of proteins, minerals and vitamins.
pg136_n0023: Nuts also contain high amounts of fats, which offer potential benefits for both brain health and function.
pg136_n0024: There are different varieties of nuts, such as cashew nuts, groundnuts, walnuts, Oysternut, Brazil nuts and almonds.
pg136_n0026: Oil seeds contain a high amount of oil.
pg136_n0027: They are also known as oil-rich seeds.
pg136_n0028: Oil is extracted from these seeds and used for various purposes, primarily as a source of edible oil used for cooking.
pg136_n0029: In contrast, whole oil seeds can be ground into flour or fine powder and used during cooking.
pg136_n0030: Examples of oil seeds are sunflower, sesame (or simsim), pumpkin seeds and cotton seeds.

pg138_n0022: Nutritive value of nuts and oil seeds
pg138_n0024: Nuts are good sources of fat, protein and fibre.
pg138_n0025: They are also rich in vitamins such as folate, niacin, vitamin E and vitamin B6 as well as minerals such as magnesium, zinc, iron, calcium and sodium.
pg138_n0026: Some nuts contain phosphorus and potassium.
pg138_n0027: Walnuts are rich in unsaturated fats like omega-3 fatty acids, which improve brain and heart health.
pg138_n0029: Oil seeds, whether whole or processed, are also known for their nutritional value.
pg138_n0030: They do not contain an appreciable amount of carbohydrates but contain a high level of B-vitamins.
pg138_n0031: They add important nutritional values to the diet owing to the presence of protein, vegetable oil and fat-soluble vitamins like vitamin A.
pg138_n0033: Uses of nuts and oil seeds
pg138_n0035: Nuts can be eaten raw or cooked.
pg138_n0036: They are also processed to make oil and other products such as peanut butter.
pg138_n0037: They can be used as ingredients for baking foods such as biscuits and cakes.
pg138_n0038: They improve food flavour and texture.
pg138_n0039: They can be served with salads or used as snacks like roasted nuts.
pg138_n0040: They are also used for garnishing and thickening sauces and stews.
pg138_n0041: Oil seeds can also be fried or roasted and eaten directly.

pg139_n0004: Methods of cooking pulses and nuts
pg139_n0006: Several methods can be used for cooking pulses, depending on the type of pulse and the desired outcome.
pg139_n0007: Pulses can be cooked by boiling, stewing and pressure cooking.
pg139_n0008: Nuts are delicious and nutritious ingredients that can be enjoyed in various ways;
pg139_n0009: Thus, they can be cooked in different ways such as frying, roasting and boiling.
pg139_n0011: Pressure cooking method: This method of moist heat uses a pressure cooker to cook food under high-pressure steam.
pg139_n0012: The food and a reasonable amount of water, depending on the type of food, are put in the pressure cooker and covered with its special tightly fitting lid.
pg139_n0013: As water boils, steam is produced.
pg139_n0014: This process increases the pressure inside the cooker.
pg139_n0015: Higher temperature and pressure cook the food very quickly.
pg139_n0016: During cooking, the cooker can regulate and maintain the pressure required to cook the food.
pg139_n0017: After cooking is complete, the pressure cooker is left for a few minutes to lower the steam pressure so that the vessel may be opened safely.
pg139_n0018: Suitable pulses for this method include dried beans, chickpeas and lentils.
pg139_im077: Labelled diagram of a pressure cooker showing the pressure regulator, overpressure regulator, sealing ring, helper handle, body, air or cover lock, cover handle, body handle, cover and vent pipe.
pg139_n0033: Each component of the pressure cooker functions as follows:
pg139_n0035: Pressure regulator: This maintains the pressure required to cook food.
pg139_n0037: Vent pipe: This allows excess steam to escape so as to maintain the required internal pressure.
pg139_n0039: Air vent or cover lock: This automatically releases air from the pressure cooker.
pg140_n0003: Sealing ring: It is a round rubber fitted around the inner part of the cover.
pg140_n0004: It forms a seal between the cover and the body of the cooker when one is cooking.
pg140_n0006: Overpressure regulator: This releases excess pressure from the cooker.
pg140_n0008: Cover handle: This is used to remove the lid from the cooker or to open the cooker.
pg140_n0010: Body handle: The handle is attached to the body of the cooker and fits underneath the cover handle.
pg140_n0012: Cover or lid: This locks over the body of the cooker.
pg140_n0013: It is fitted with a sealing ring for proper closing.
pg140_n0015: Points to remember when using a pressure cooker
pg140_n0019: An adequate amount of water should be used to ensure that sufficient steam builds up inside the cooker.
pg140_n0022: No more than two-thirds of the solid food capacity and no more than half of the liquid capacity should be in the cooker.
pg140_n0023: If these amounts are exceeded, the control valve will fail.
pg140_n0026: Ensure that the lid is correctly locked in place before starting the cooking process.
pg140_n0029: Place the pressure gauge in position and allow pressure to build up to the desired level.
pg140_n0030: A steady hissing sound indicates that pressure has built up.
pg140_n0033: Lower the heat to maintain the desired pressure and cook for the correct time.
pg140_n0034: Timing should commence once the pressure has been reached.
pg140_n0037: When cooking time is completed, turn off the heat and allow the pressure to fall either by leaving the cooker at room temperature or by pouring a gentle stream of cold water over it.
pg140_n0038: Never attempt to open the lid or remove the pressure gauge before the pressure has come to normal.
pg140_n0040: Advantages of using a pressure cooker
pg140_n0045: It is cost effective on fuel use, and it requires less time and energy to cook food, leading to lower energy consumption and reduced cooking costs.
pg140_n0048: It is suitable for pulses with hard coats as they easily become tender during pressure cooking.
pg141_n0005: Pressure cooking reduces the need for constant monitoring and stirring during cooking, allowing you to set it up and leave it until the cooking is complete.
pg141_n0008: Pressure cookers can be used for a wide range of dishes including beans, cowpeas and pigeon peas.
pg141_n0011: The shorter cooking time and minimal liquid usage in a pressure cooker help retain more nutrients such as vitamins and minerals in the food compared to longer cooking methods that may cause nutrient loss.
pg141_n0014: Due to reduced energy usage and water retention, pressure cooker contributes to a lower overall environmental impact.
pg141_n0020: High-quality pressure cookers can be more expensive than traditional cooking pots.
pg141_n0023: While modern pressure cookers have built-in safety features, there is still a risk of misuse, especially if the safety features are not understood or followed properly.
pg141_n0026: If the pressure cooker is not used correctly or if there is insufficient liquid, there is a risk of burning the food, which can be challenging to clean.
pg141_n0030: Limited cooking space and the size of a pressure cooker can limit the amount of food that can be cooked at once.
pg141_n0031: Cooking larger quantities of food may require multiple batches.
pg141_n0035: Difficulty in adjusting seasonings, once the lid is closed and pressure builds, causes difficult in adjusting seasonings or making changes to the dish.
pg141_n0036: Seasoning adjustments are better made before cooking.

pg154_n0009: Proper nutrition is important for the body to stay active and perform its functions effectively.
pg154_n0010: It is a result of consuming a balanced meal, which is required for life.
pg154_n0011: A person who takes proper nutrition can participate in various economic activities and raise his or her standard of living.
pg154_n0012: In this chapter, you will learn about the concept of proper nutrition, the importance of proper nutrition on health and the relationship between diet, health and physical activities.
pg154_n0013: You will also learn about various eating disorders.
pg154_n0014: The competencies developed will enable you to make informed dietary choices and prevent Non-Communicable Diseases(NCDs), and eating disorders, you will also be able to educate the community at large.
pg154_n0021: Proper nutrition means getting a balanced meal together with performing regular physical activities such as running and walking.
pg154_n0022: Good health depends on proper nutrition.
pg154_n0023: Proper nutrition is essential for maintaining and promoting optimal health and well-being throughout life.
pg154_n0024: Making informed dietary choices and adopting healthy eating habits are crucial steps in enhancing overall health and preventing nutrition-related health disorders.
pg154_n0026: Proper nutrition is also important in achieving healthy lifestyle.
pg154_n0027: It refers to an individual’s way of living, including behaviours and choices that lower the risk of becoming ill or dying early.
pg154_n0028: A healthy lifestyle includes the following aspects:
pg154_n0032: Moderate use of sweetened foods and drinks: These foods contain large
pg155_n0005: Sweetened foods and drinks contribute to health problems such as overweight, obesity, heart attack, stroke, kidney stones and some types of cancers.
pg155_n0006: It is advised to use them in moderate amounts.
pg155_n0010: Minimal use of junk foods: These foods are high in fat, sugar and salt and are low in protein, vitamin or mineral nutrients.
pg155_n0011: Examples of junk foods include carbonated beverages, gum and fried fast foods.
pg155_n0014: Non-use of tobacco and alcohol: Smoked, chewed, or sniffed tobacco products are harmful to health as they contribute to an increased risk of non-communicable diseases.
pg155_n0017: Achieving and maintaining a healthy body weight: A healthy body weight enables a person to feel fit and energetic.
pg155_n0018: It also reduces the risk of non-communicable diseases.
pg155_n0021: Maintaining personal and food hygiene and safety: It is important to maintain good personal and food hygiene and safety when preparing food to prevent illnesses.
pg155_n0025: Proper nutrition has several benefits for our bodies as follows:
pg155_n0027: Strengthening the body’s immune system: Proper nutrition builds body immunity.
pg155_n0028: A body with strong immunity will not be affected easily by diseases.
pg155_n0029: Strong immunity will enable a person to participate actively in various productive activities.
pg155_n0031: Maintain the required energy level in the body: The body needs energy to perform various activities.
pg155_n0032: For example, the digestion process requires energy.
pg155_n0033: Eating a balanced meal enables the body to obtain the energy needed to perform various functions.
pg155_n0035: Improves physical and mental health: Proper nutrition makes the body active and strong.
pg155_n0036: Eating meals that contain adequate amounts of nutrients allows a person to have a healthy mind, hence increasing thinking and reasoning capabilities.
pg155_n0038: Helps a person to live longer: Consuming a meal rich in nutrients increases lifespan.
pg155_n0039: Healthy eating makes the body strong and prevents certain diseases.
pg155_n0040: It is better to follow good eating habits to remain healthier.
pg155_n0042: Helps in maintaining healthy body weight: Proper nutrition helps an individual to achieve the required body weight.
pg155_n0043: The required body weight is achieved through adequate nutrient intake and regular physical activities.
pg156_n0003: Improves growth and development: Proper nutrition is crucial during growth and development stages, especially in childhood and adolescence.
pg156_n0004: Essential nutrients support proper physical growth.
pg156_n0005: Undernutrition during childhood can lead to stunted growth.
pg156_n0007: Improves bone health: A healthy meal rich in Calcium and vitamin D is crucial for maintaining good bone health and preventing conditions such as osteomalacia, which is characterized by softening and weakening of bones due to the deficiency of vitamin D, Calcium or phosphorus.
pg156_n0008: Adequate intake of these nutrients, along with other bone-supporting nutrients, including vitamin K, magnesium and protein is essential for strong and healthy bones throughout life.
pg156_n0010: Relationship between diet, physical activity and health
pg156_n0012: A diet refers to the food that a person normally eats.
pg156_n0013: It is sometimes changed to control the intake of certain foods to prevent, treat or manage certain health conditions.
pg156_n0014: This kind of diet is known as a special diet.
pg156_n0015: Examples of special diets include low-fat, low-carbohydrate, low salt and low-sugar diets.
pg156_n0017: Diet, physical activity, and health are interconnected.
pg156_n0018: When they are balanced, they have a positive impact on the overall well-being of a person.
pg156_n0019: Physical activity is described as any movement of the body caused by skeletal muscles; such a movement requires the use of energy.
pg156_n0020: Performing regular physical activities reduces the risk of becoming overweight and obese which are risky factors for the development of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), also known as chronic diseases, such as coronary heart diseases, type 2 diabetes and some cancers.
pg156_n0021: Examples of physical activities are walking, running, dancing, swimming, and gardening.
pg156_n0023: The following aspects show the relationship between diet, physical activity and health:
pg156_n0027: A balanced meal and regular physical activities are vital for a healthy bodyweight.
pg156_n0028: A nutrient-rich meal along with regular physical activities can prevent excessive weight gain, thus maintaining ideal body weight.
pg156_n0031: A balanced meal and physical activity benefit heart health.
pg156_n0032: A low-fat and low-sodium meals and regular physical activity can lower blood pressure, reduce cholesterol, and lower the risk of heart disease.
pg156_n0035: Proper nutrition, especially an adequate intake of calcium and vitamin D, is essential for maintaining good teeth and bone health.
pg156_n0036: When combined with physical activities, it further supports bone strength and overall well-being.
pg157_n0006: A balanced meal with various vitamins and minerals supports the immune system, making the body more resilient to infections and illnesses.
pg157_n0007: Performing regular physical activities is also associated with enhanced immune system functions.
pg157_n0011: A balanced meal and physical activity have a great impact on mental health.
pg157_n0012: Nutrient-rich foods and regular physical activity reduces depression and anxiety risk, improve mood and boost cognitive function.
pg157_n0016: Proper nutrition and regular physical activities can prevent or manage non-communicable diseases such as type 2 diabetes and some cancers.
pg157_n0017: A healthy lifestyle lowers the risk of developing these conditions.
pg157_n0021: A balanced meal and regular physical activity improve sleep.
pg157_n0022: They promote better sleep patterns, thus benefiting the overall physical health.
pg157_n0026: A healthy lifestyle with balanced meals and physical activity is linked to longer life and reduce the risk of premature death.

pg159_n0005: An eating disorder is a serious health condition caused by avoidance or excessive consumption of food.
pg159_n0006: It affects weight and body shape.
pg159_n0007: This can lead to bad eating habits that may significantly impair physical health and normal functioning of the body.
pg159_n0008: These disorders are more common among teenage girls and young women than among boys and men.
pg159_n0009: If not managed effectively, eating disorders can result in long-term problems and, in some cases, can lead to death.
pg159_n0010: The most common eating disorders are anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating and pica.
pg159_n0014: Eating disorders can affect people of all ages, backgrounds and genders.
pg159_n0015: However, eating disorders often occur during adolescence and may also develop during childhood or later in life.
pg159_n0016: Some of the factors which may lead to the development of eating disorders have been identified, as follows:
pg159_n0021: Genetics and family history: Eating disorders are more likely to occur in people whose parents or siblings have an eating disorder.
pg159_n0025: Gender: Eating disorders are more prevalent in females than in males because females are more conscious of their body images.
pg159_n0026: However, it can affect individuals of any gender
pg159_n0030: Age: Eating disorders often emerge during adolescence and early adulthood.
pg159_n0031: The pressure to conform to societal beauty standards and navigate body image changes during these developmental stages can contribute to the risk.
pg159_n0035: Body image dissatisfaction: Poor body image or dissatisfaction with one’s appearance can be a significant risk factor for developing an eating disorder.
pg159_n0039: Other mental health issues: Stress, anxiety, depression and other mental health issues can increase the likelihood of an eating disorder.
pg159_n0043: A history of weight bullying: People who have been bullied for their weight are more likely to develop eating disorders.
pg159_n0044: These include people who have been made to feel ashamed of their weight by peers, healthcare professionals, coaches or family members.
pg159_n0048: Social media pressure: Exposure to unrealistic body images and unhealthy messages about dieting and appearance on social media can impact body image and contribute to the risk of eating disorders.
pg160_n0003: (viii) Occupations: Certain occupations can increase the risk of eating disorders as certain body image is considered as ideal.
pg160_n0004: Some occupations that may increase the risk of eating disorders include athletics, fashion modelling, acting, dancing, and performing arts.
pg160_n0006: Note: It is important to note that having one or more of these factors does not necessarily mean someone will develop an eating disorder, but they may increase its risk.
pg160_n0008: Characteristics of people with eating disorders
pg160_n0010: Individuals with eating disorders often exhibit a range of physical, emotional and behavioural characteristics.
pg160_n0011: It is important to note that each person experiencing an eating disorder is unique.
pg160_n0013: The following are some common characteristics observed in people with eating disorders:
pg160_n0015: Distorted perception of their body image: Some people with eating disorders often have a distorted perception of their body size and shape.
pg160_n0016: For example, they may perceive themselves as overweight even when they are significantly underweight.
pg160_n0018: Restrictive eating patterns: In a condition like anorexia nervosa, individuals severely restrict their food intake, leading to significant weight loss and malnutrition.
pg160_n0019: They may avoid certain food groups or severely limit their overall calorie intake.
pg160_n0021: Changes in eating habits: There may be a noticeable change in eating habits, such as eating alone, avoiding eating in public with others, or making excuses to avoid eating.
pg160_n0022: People with binge eating disorder engage in excessive eating.
pg160_n0024: Social withdrawal: People with eating disorders may withdraw from social activities and isolate themselves from friends and family.
pg160_n0026: Emotional and behavioural changes: Mood swings, anxiety, depression, and feelings of guilt or shame are common emotional characteristics.
pg160_n0028: Development of physical signs: Physical signs of eating disorders can include rapid weight loss, dizziness, weakness, hair loss, dry skin, and changes in menstrual patterns (amenorrhea) among women.
pg160_n0030: Excessive exercise: Some individuals may engage in excessive exercise as a way of controlling weight and shape.
pg161_n0005: Eating disorders are a group of related conditions involving extreme food and weight issues, but each disorder has unique symptoms and diagnosis criteria.
pg161_n0006: The common eating disorders include anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating and pica.
pg161_n0010: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by an abnormally low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted perception of weight.
pg161_n0011: It involves restriction of energy foods, which leads to significantly low body weight in relation to the individual’s age, sex, and height.
pg161_n0012: This restriction is often secondary to an intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, despite the individual’s low body weight.
pg161_n0013: Anorexia nervosa is most likely a well-known eating disorder.
pg161_n0014: It generally develops during adolescence or young adulthood and tends to affect more women than men.
pg161_n0015: People with anorexia nervosa generally view themselves as overweight, even if they are critically underweight.
pg161_n0016: They tend to constantly monitor their body weight, avoid eating certain types of foods, and severely restrict their calorie intake.
pg161_n0020: This is an eating disorder characterized by consuming a large amount of food in a short period.
pg161_n0021: Thereafter, the person tries to induce vomiting or use diet pills and other medications, fast, or do excessive exercise to avoid weight gain.
pg161_n0022: If it is not treated, bulimia nervosa can lead to nutritional deficiencies and may have fatal complications.
pg161_n0023: Bulimics are usually ashamed of their behaviour and tend to hide this condition from others.
pg161_n0027: This is an eating disorder characterized by consuming large quantities of food in a short period, similar to bulimia nervosa.
pg161_n0028: However, individuals with this condition do not engage in vomiting, excessive exercise, or other behaviours.
pg161_n0029: Individuals with this condition lack a sense of control over eating behaviour.
pg161_n0030: They usually eat rapidly until they feel uncomfortably full, even when they are not physically hungry.
pg161_n0031: These people are often accompanied by feelings of guilt, shame and distress.
pg161_n0032: Individuals with BED report feelings of embarrassment on the quantity of food consumed, and thus will often refuse to eat in public.
pg161_n0033: These people often consume excessive amounts of food and may not make nutritious food choices.
pg161_n0034: This may increase the risk for obesity and non-communicable diseases such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes.
pg162_n0005: Pica is an eating disorder which involves eating non-food items that lack nutritional value, such as soil, chalk, charcoal or even ice.
pg162_n0006: This condition is most commonly observed in children and pregnant women.
pg162_n0007: Pica can be dangerous as it may lead to serious health problems including poisoning, infections, gut injuries, and nutrient deficiency.

pg162_n0019: Prevention and control of eating disorders
pg162_n0021: Controlling eating disorders involves collective actions that address physical, psychological and emotional aspects of the condition.
pg162_n0022: Eating disorders can have severe consequences on a person’s physical and emotional well-being.
pg162_n0023: While there is no exact way to prevent eating disorders, developing healthy eating habits can be helpful.
pg162_n0024: It is worth noting that every individual’s journey to recover from an eating disorder is unique.
pg162_n0025: Therefore, seeking professional help from healthcare providers specialised in eating disorder treatment is crucial.
pg162_n0026: Early action to address these problems can significantly improve the chances of successful recovery.
pg162_n0027: The following are the ways of controlling eating disorders:
pg162_n0031: A healthcare professional may conduct a thorough medical assessment to evaluate the individual’s overall health, identify any medical complications resulting from the eating disorder, and develop a suitable treatment plan.
pg162_n0032: Medical treatment may involve addressing any nutritional conditions, stabilising weight, and managing any physical health issues related to the eating disorder.
pg163_n0006: It is important for individuals or communities to be provided with information and knowledge about nutrition, dietary habits and the importance of a balanced diet.
pg163_n0007: Nutrition education aims to promote healthy eating habits, improve overall health, prevent diet-related illnesses and encourage good food choices.
pg163_n0008: Involving family members in nutrition education can enhance understanding and management of eating disorders.
pg163_n0009: Nutrition education can be provided in communities, schools and health facilities by nutritionists.
pg163_n0010: However, peer group educators are also effective.
pg163_n0011: Media such as television, radio, posters, fliers and social networks can be used to create nutrition awareness.

pg163_n0019: (i) Describe the mechanisms for preventing and controlling anorexia nervosa that you will present to them.
pg163_n0020: (ii) Explain the common cause of this disorder.
pg164_n0007: Psychotherapy, also known as talk therapy, is a crucial component of eating disorder treatment that is done by mental health professionals.
pg164_n0008: It involves regular personal interaction to help an individual change bad behaviour.
pg164_n0009: Family-based therapy is among the treatments commonly used to treat eating disorders.
pg164_n0010: These therapies can help individuals develop healthier thoughts and emotions as well as better behaviours on food, body image and self-esteem.
pg164_n0014: Working with a nutritionist or registered dietitian who specializes in eating disorders can be beneficial in creating a balanced and healthy meal plan.
pg164_n0015: Nutrition counselling helps individuals develop a healthier relationship with food and establish regular eating patterns and improved behaviours.
pg164_n0019: It is very common for eating disorders to occur with other mental health conditions, such as depression and anxiety.
pg164_n0020: Identifying and treating any existing disorders is crucial for comprehensive recovery.
pg164_n0024: Identifying and minimizing triggers that increase disordered eating behaviours is important.
pg164_n0025: This includes limiting exposure to social media or content that promotes unrealistic body ideas or unhealthy eating behaviours.

pg009_n0008_easy_read: Food and nutrition are important parts of human life and overall well-being.
pg009_n0009_easy_read:
It is important to understand the basic ideas of food and nutrition.
This helps us make informed choices about the food we eat and how it affects our bodies.
pg009_n0010_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn about:
- the meaning of food and nutrition
- the importance of food
- the relationship between Food and Human Nutrition and other subjects
pg009_n0011_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you:
- keep healthy eating habits for life
- avoid health problems linked to nutrition
pg009_n0014_easy_read: How food and nutrition help in our life
pg009_n0018_easy_read:
Food is anything you can eat or drink.
It can be solid, semi-solid or liquid.
When the body eats, digests and takes in food, food gives the body important substances called nutrients.
pg009_n0019_easy_read:
Nutrients help a person to:
- stay alive
- get energy
- grow
- repair worn-out tissues
- protect the body from diseases
pg009_n0020_easy_read: Food comes from plants and animals.
pg009_n0021_easy_read: Food can be eaten raw or in a processed form.
pg009_n0023_easy_read:
Nutrition is the process of taking in food.
The body changes food into energy and other important nutrients needed for life.
pg009_n0024_easy_read: Nutrition is about how the body uses nutrients to feed itself and do different functions.
pg009_n0025_easy_read:
Nutrition is the study of the body's processes for:
- growth
- maintenance
- repair of worn-out tissues
These processes help the body stay healthy.
pg009_n0029_easy_read:
It is important to understand the functions of food.
This helps people make informed food choices that support good health and well-being throughout life.
pg009_n0030_easy_read: The following are the importance of food:
pg010_n0003_easy_read: Providing energy to the body: The body needs energy for many activities.
pg010_n0004_easy_read: Foods with a lot of carbohydrates and fats are the main sources of energy for the body.
pg010_n0006_easy_read: Building and repairing body cells and worn-out tissues: Body tissues keep breaking down and dying. They need repair and replacement to keep the body healthy.
pg010_n0007_easy_read: Foods rich in proteins, minerals and water are needed to build and replace body cells and worn-out tissues.
pg010_n0009_easy_read: Regulating body processes: Foods with fats, proteins, minerals, vitamins and water help to regulate body processes. For example, they help to keep body temperature steady and activate enzymes.
pg010_n0011_easy_read: Protecting the body against diseases: Food gives the body vitamins and minerals. These help to protect the body from diseases.
pg010_n0012_easy_read: Vitamins and minerals are also important for digestion and other body processes.
pg010_n0013_easy_read: Examples of protective foods are fruits and vegetables.
pg010_n0015_easy_read: Strengthening social relations: Eating together helps people build social relations.
pg010_n0016_easy_read: Food helps bring people from different classes, communities and religions together.
pg010_n0018_easy_read: Identification: Food can help identify people from different backgrounds, such as ethnic or cultural backgrounds.
pg010_n0019_easy_read: For example, liking bananas among the people of Bukoba and Kilimanjaro shows part of their cultural identity.
pg010_n0023_easy_read:
Food can be classified in different ways:
- by the function it performs in the body
- by its chemical composition
- by the chemical properties of nutrients
- by its source or origin
pg010_n0027_easy_read:
Using this criterion, foods are classified as:
- energy-giving foods
- body-building foods
- protective foods
pg010_n0029_easy_read: Energy-giving foods: Foods rich in carbohydrates and fats give the body energy. This energy is needed for physical activities and for the body to work properly.
pg010_n0030_easy_read: These foods are called energy-giving foods.
pg010_n0031_easy_read:
Foods that are good sources of energy include:
- cereals
- roots
- tubers
- fats, such as butter, ghee and oils
pg010_n0033_easy_read: Body-building foods: One of the most important functions of food is to build the body.
pg010_n0034_easy_read: Foods rich in protein are called body-building foods.
pg010_n0035_easy_read: These foods help to maintain life. They also help the body grow and repair damaged body tissues.
pg011_n0003_easy_read: Foods come from animals and plants.
pg011_n0004_easy_read:
Good sources of animal protein are:
- milk
- meat
- eggs
- fish

Good sources of plant protein are:
- pulses
- nuts
pg011_n0005_easy_read:
People consider animal protein sources to be higher quality than plant protein sources.
Soybeans are an exception because they contain higher-quality protein.
pg011_n0007_easy_read:
Protective foods:
Foods with a lot of minerals and vitamins are called protective foods.
pg011_n0008_easy_read: Protective foods protect the body against diseases.
pg011_n0009_easy_read:
Examples of protective foods are:
- fruits
- vegetables
pg011_n0013_easy_read:
The chemical composition of food is important.
It shows how the body uses the food.
pg011_n0014_easy_read: This classification is based on the type and amount of nutrients in the food.
pg011_n0015_easy_read:
Carbohydrates, proteins and lipids are the major chemical components of food.
This is because foods contain them in large quantities.
pg011_n0016_easy_read:
Vitamins and minerals are the minor chemical components of food.
This is because foods contain them in smaller quantities.
pg011_n0020_easy_read:
In this type of classification, food is classified by the chemical properties of nutrients.
For example, nutrients can be organic or inorganic.
pg011_n0021_easy_read: Nutrients such as carbohydrates, protein, fat and vitamins contain carbon elements.
pg011_n0022_easy_read:
These nutrients are called organic nutrients.
Nutrients that do not contain carbon elements, such as minerals, are called inorganic nutrients.
pg011_n0026_easy_read: Food can be classified by its origin, or source.
pg011_n0027_easy_read:
Foods that come from animals are called animal food sources.
Foods that come from plants are called plant food sources.
pg011_n0031_easy_read:
Watch reliable online videos or read other sources about the classification of food.
Then explain how understanding food classification can help you improve your health.

pg012_n0014_easy_read:

- give energy
- help the body grow and repair body tissues
- protect the body from disease

pg027_n0032_easy_read: If fruit juice is exposed to air, it may lose vitamin C.
pg028_n0003_easy_read: You can keep nutrients in food during food preparation in the following ways:
pg028_n0007_easy_read:
When you peel foods like potatoes, carrots and fruits, use a sharp knife.
Peel them thinly.
This helps you avoid losing the nutrients under the peel.
pg028_n0010_easy_read:
Wash fruits and vegetables before you chop them.
This helps stop vitamins leaking into the water.
pg028_n0011_easy_read: Use a sharp knife when you chop food.
pg028_n0014_easy_read:
Do not leave vegetables in direct sunlight.
This helps prevent the loss of vitamins, such as vitamin C.
pg028_n0017_easy_read: Prepare fruits and vegetables only a few minutes before serving.
pg028_n0020_easy_read:
Do not soak fruits and vegetables.
Water-soluble vitamins can leak into the soaking water.
pg028_n0024_easy_read: When some foods are cooked in water, nutrients dissolve in the water.
pg028_n0025_easy_read: If you throw away the water, you lose these nutrients.
pg028_n0026_easy_read: Cooking leafy vegetables for too long can destroy some vitamins.
pg028_n0028_easy_read: You can keep nutrients in food during cooking in the following ways:
pg028_n0032_easy_read:
Cook leafy vegetables for a short time, just before serving.
Do not overcook them.
Overcooking causes the loss of some nutrients.
pg028_n0035_easy_read:
Cook food with a little water.
Serve the food with its liquid.
This helps you avoid losing water-soluble vitamins.
pg028_n0038_easy_read:
Prepare only enough food for the time.
This helps avoid leftovers that will need reheating.
Reheating causes loss of nutrients.
pg028_n0041_easy_read:
Cook vegetables for a short time.
This helps reduce the loss of nutrients that are damaged by heat, such as B vitamins and vitamin C.
pg028_n0044_easy_read:
Cover the food when cooking.
Some water-soluble vitamins, like B-vitamins and vitamin C, can evaporate.
pg028_n0047_easy_read:
Do not use bicarbonate of soda or ashes in cooking.
They destroy many vitamins, such as vitamins C, D, B<math><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and B<math><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math>.

pg029_n0005_easy_read: Moisture also causes iodine to be lost.
pg029_n0006_easy_read: When milk is left in the sun, it loses B vitamins.
pg029_n0008_easy_read: You can keep nutrients in food during storage in these ways:
pg029_n0012_easy_read: Store fruits and vegetables for a short time. This helps them keep their freshness, nutrients, flavour and overall quality.
pg029_n0015_easy_read: Keep milk in covered, coloured containers. This helps prevent loss of vitamin B2.
pg029_n0018_easy_read: Store food in a cool place and away from direct sunlight. Direct sunlight can cause the loss of nutrients such as vitamins B2 and C.
pg029_n0021_easy_read: Store iodized salt in a cool place. Heat reduces the iodine in the salt.

pg030_n0005_easy_read: A meal means all the foods eaten at 1 time, such as breakfast, lunch or supper.
pg030_n0007_easy_read: A dish is food prepared in a particular way as part of a meal.
pg030_n0008_easy_read: A balanced meal has a variety of foods from all food groups.
pg030_n0009_easy_read:
A balanced meal should have enough nutrients in the right amounts.
The body needs these nutrients for:
- growth
- repairing damaged tissues
- keeping good health
pg030_n0010_easy_read:
These nutrients are:
- carbohydrates
- fats
- proteins
- minerals
- vitamins
pg030_n0011_easy_read:
No single food can give all nutrients in the right amount.
Good nutrition depends on eating a variety of foods from all food groups.
pg030_n0012_easy_read: A balanced meal should also include enough water and roughage.

pg031_n0006_easy_read:
A balanced meal is very important for the body.
It includes foods from all food groups.
These foods give essential nutrients for:
- growth
- repair of damaged body tissues
- strengthening the body's immune system to help prevent disease
pg031_n0007_easy_read:
It is important to eat a balanced meal at least 3 times a day.
This helps the body get all the nutrients it needs to work normally.
pg031_n0008_easy_read:
A balanced meal also helps prevent depression and anxiety.
It also helps people think better.
pg031_n0009_easy_read:
A balanced meal also helps children and adolescents grow and develop.
This is important because they are still growing.
pg031_n0010_easy_read: For elderly people, a balanced meal helps maintain and repair worn-out tissues.
pg031_n0014_easy_read:
Meals should be planned for all family members.
This helps each person get the right foods and the right amount of nutrients for their food preferences and nutritional needs.
pg031_n0015_easy_read: When planning family meals, consider these points:
pg031_n0017_easy_read:
Nutrient adequacy:
Make sure the meal contains all the nutrients.
pg031_n0018_easy_read: This can be done by including foods from all food groups.
pg031_n0019_easy_read:
Also think about dietary fibre when planning meals.
Dietary fibre helps digestion.
pg031_n0021_easy_read:
Food variety:
Food variety is important because it:
- helps avoid eating the same foods all the time
- helps prevent dietary deficiency
- makes the dish more appetising
pg031_n0022_easy_read:
You can do this by:
- using different cooking methods
- including foods with different flavours
- including foods with different textures
- including foods with different colours
pg031_n0024_easy_read:
Seasonal availability of food:
It is wise to choose foods that are in season because they are:
- fresh
- nutritious
- cheap
pg031_n0025_easy_read: Foods that are out of season are often expensive.
pg031_n0026_easy_read: Also, most out-of-season foods may not be fresh because they have been processed or stored for a long time.
pg031_n0027_easy_read:
Examples of seasonal foods are:
- vegetables
- fruits
pg031_n0029_easy_read:
Individual body needs:
This includes a person's:
- age
- sex
- occupation
- state of the body
pg031_n0035_easy_read:
The meal prepared should match the age of each family member.
This is because nutritional needs are different at different life stages, such as:
- children
- adolescents
- adults
- the elderly
pg031_n0036_easy_read: For example, children need more protein foods than adults because they grow quickly.
pg031_n0041_easy_read: A person's sex can affect meal planning.
pg031_n0042_easy_read:
Women of Reproductive Age (WRA) need more iron-rich foods than men.
This helps replace the blood lost during menstruation.
pg031_n0043_easy_read: Usually, adolescents and adult males need more energy than females.
pg032_n0004_easy_read: The meal should meet the body's needs for the kind of work the person does.
pg032_n0005_easy_read: For example, people who sit most of the time need less energy-giving food than manual workers.
pg032_n0008_easy_read: This factor includes different body conditions, such as disease, pregnancy and lactation.
pg032_n0009_easy_read: These conditions affect how much food a person needs and how the body uses nutrients.
pg032_n0010_easy_read: For example, sick people need more proteins and vitamins. This helps recovery and strengthens the immune system.
pg032_n0011_easy_read: People with type 2 diabetes do not need foods with a lot of sugar in their diet. Pregnant women need more folate and iron in their meals to help prevent birth defects and anaemia.
pg032_n0014_easy_read: The family food you prepare also depends on the time available for shopping, preparing, cooking and serving food.
pg032_n0015_easy_read: For example, a person can choose fresh beans instead of dry beans because dry beans take a long time to cook.
pg032_n0016_easy_read: A person with a gas cooker or an electric cooker can prepare many dishes in a short time.
pg032_n0017_easy_read: In contrast, a person using a charcoal stove may not be able to do this, unless the person uses several charcoal stoves at the same time.
pg032_n0020_easy_read: The budget for family meals decides the type, quality and quantity of food to buy.
pg032_n0021_easy_read: For many families, foods such as beef, chicken and fish can be too expensive.
pg032_n0022_easy_read: So, a family can buy other foods, such as sardines or offal, that have similar nutrients.
pg032_n0025_easy_read: You should consider the kitchenware and equipment available for preparing, cooking and serving food, and also the storage facilities.
pg032_n0028_easy_read: A meal should be prepared to suit the weather conditions.
pg032_n0029_easy_read: For example, hot foods and drinks, such as soup and tea, help to keep the body warm in cold weather.
pg032_n0032_easy_read:
Meals should be planned for the right time of day, such as:
- morning
- afternoon
- evening
pg032_n0033_easy_read: For example, supper should be light because the person is getting ready to go to bed.
pg032_n0034_easy_read: At night, the body needs little energy because it will be resting.
pg032_n0036_easy_read: Religion, cultural values, traditional beliefs and taboos:
pg032_n0037_easy_read: Religion, cultural values, traditional beliefs and taboos decide what people should cook and eat.
pg032_n0038_easy_read: When planning meals, you should consider these beliefs so the meals are acceptable in the family or local area.

pg035_n0008_easy_read: The kitchen is 1 of the important places in a home.
pg035_n0009_easy_read: The kitchen should have the right equipment for preparing and cooking food well.
pg035_n0010_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn about:
- the kitchen
- hygiene in preparing and cooking food
- safety in the kitchen
pg035_n0011_easy_read:
The skills you learn will help you:
- take proper care of the kitchen
- avoid accidents
- prepare, cook, and serve food in a hygienic way
pg035_n0017_easy_read:
A kitchen is a room or area where people prepare, cook, and sometimes serve food.
It can be inside or outside a house or commercial building.
pg035_n0018_easy_read: People also do other related activities in the kitchen, such as washing utensils.
pg035_n0019_easy_read:
A kitchen should be well planned.
This helps people work better and save time and energy.
pg035_n0020_easy_read:
When a kitchen is well planned, the utensils are arranged in the right order.
This creates a continuous work area.
It matches the order and stages of the main kitchen activities.
pg035_n0021_easy_read:
It is important to arrange fixed equipment in the right order for kitchen activities.
This saves working time and avoids unnecessary movement.
pg035_n0022_easy_read: A kitchen can be built inside or outside the main house.
pg035_n0025_easy_read: There are 2 main types of kitchens in homes.
pg035_n0026_easy_read: The 2 main types are open kitchens and separate kitchens.
pg036_n0005_easy_read: In this type, people can see the kitchen openly from the dining room or living room.
pg036_n0006_easy_read: There is no separate wall, partition, or door.
pg036_n0007_easy_read: An open kitchen lets hosts or cooks talk with guests while they prepare meals.
pg036_n0008_easy_read:
With an open kitchen, it is easy to:
- prepare meals
- replace meals
- remove dirty utensils from the dining table
pg036_n0009_easy_read:
It is also easy to see:
- unwashed dishes
- scattered utensils
- food scraps
pg036_n0010_easy_read: So, this type of kitchen needs constant cleaning to keep the kitchen clean and hygienic.
pg036_n0011_easy_read: There are 2 types of open kitchen, as described below:
pg036_n0013_easy_read:
Kitchen open to the dining room:
In this type, the kitchen opens into the dining room.
pg036_n0014_easy_read: There is no separate wall or door. A person in the dining room can see everything in the kitchen, as shown in Figure 3.1.
pg036_n0015_easy_read: Usually, there is no privacy during meal preparation. People sitting in the dining room can see food preparation and cooking in the kitchen.
pg036_n0017_easy_read: Figure 3.1: Kitchen open to the dining room
pg036_n0019_easy_read:
Kitchen open to the living room:
In this type, the kitchen is joined to the living room.
pg036_n0020_easy_read: People can see it clearly from the living room.
pg036_n0021_easy_read:
This type of kitchen makes it easy to do other activities while preparing meals, such as:
- watching television
- spending time with other family members
- spending time with guests
pg036_n0022_easy_read: In some houses, this type of kitchen has an area where food is served, as shown in Figure 3.2.
pg037_n0003_easy_read: Figure 3.2: Kitchen open to the living room
pg037_n0007_easy_read: This type of kitchen can be inside the main house (enclosed) or outside the main house (isolated).
pg037_n0008_easy_read:
A separate kitchen gives privacy when you prepare meals.
It also stops heat, steam and smoke from going into the house.
pg037_n0009_easy_read:
Separate kitchens have a more traditional and practical layout.
They are good for people who prefer a clear separation between cooking space and living space.
pg038_n0007_easy_read:
A good kitchen has several important features.
These features make the kitchen efficient, useful, and pleasant to work in.
pg038_n0008_easy_read: These are the qualities of a good kitchen:
pg038_n0012_easy_read: The kitchen should be in a place where enough sunlight and air can enter.
pg038_n0015_easy_read: The kitchen walls should have a smooth material that is easy to clean.
pg038_n0016_easy_read:
The kitchen walls and ceiling should have bright colours.
Bright colours reflect light in the room.
pg038_n0019_easy_read: The kitchen floor should be made of non-slippery materials that are easy to clean, such as cement and tiles.
pg039_n0010_easy_read:
The kitchen should have large equipment in convenient places for quick and easy movement.
This equipment includes:
- cookers
- sinks
- cupboards
- refrigerators
pg039_n0013_easy_read: The kitchen should have windows that are large enough for proper air circulation.
pg039_n0014_easy_read:
Ventilation is important because it removes:
- smoke
- smell
- excess heat
from the kitchen.
pg039_n0017_easy_read: The kitchen should have enough lighting for safe food preparation and cooking.
pg039_n0018_easy_read:
A good kitchen has both natural light and artificial light.
This helps you see clearly during the day and at night.
pg039_n0021_easy_read: The kitchen should have a sink with taps that give a good supply of hot and cold water.
pg039_n0022_easy_read:
The sink should be fixed directly under the kitchen window.
This gives the user enough natural light and fresh air while working at the sink.
pg039_n0025_easy_read: A kitchen with a good drainage system helps keep the kitchen hygienic.
pg039_n0028_easy_read: The kitchen should have a wastebin for collecting rubbish.

pg040_n0005_easy_read: Kitchen equipment means tools, appliances, and utensils for preparing food, cooking, and other kitchen tasks.
pg040_n0006_easy_read: The right kitchen equipment can make cooking easier and more enjoyable.
pg040_n0007_easy_read:
There are 3 types of kitchen equipment:

(vi) Knives include:

pg040_n0024_easy_read: Labour-saving equipment are appliances that help people prepare food, cook, and serve food faster. This saves time and energy.
pg040_n0025_easy_read: These devices help people work faster and do tasks with less physical effort.
pg040_n0026_easy_read:
Some examples of labour-saving kitchen equipment are:
